questions.question: What does 'git add' do, and what is the difference between 'git add .' and 'git add filename'?
questions.title: git add: Staging Changes
questions.direct_answer: **`git add`** moves changes from the **working directory** into the **staging area** (the index), the zone where you assemble your next commit. **`git add .`** stages every modified and new file under the current directory; **`git add filename`** stages just that one file. Use the filename form (or **`git add -p`**) to build focused commits and avoid accidentally staging secrets.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands Git's three-tree model and can craft deliberate, focused commits instead of dumping everything
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Running git add . by reflex and committing secrets (application.properties with a DB password, .env) or build output
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention git add -p to stage individual hunks and git add -u to stage modified/deleted files without new untracked ones

sections.title: The Staging Area Is Where You Assemble a Commit
sections.content:
The **staging area** (or **index**) is Git's middle layer between your working directory and the committed history. Think of it as a shipping dock: you place exactly the items you want on the dock, arrange them, then load the truck (commit).

**`git add`** is how you put files on that dock. This is what lets you make one clean commit even when you've changed ten files but only three belong together. **`git add .`** is the broad stroke — it stages everything (modified and new) under the current directory tree. **`git add filename`** is surgical — it stages only what you name. This three-tree design (working directory → staging area → repository) is exactly what makes Git history read like a story instead of a dump of unrelated changes.

sections.title: git add . vs git add filename
sections.content:
| Aspect | `git add .` | `git add filename` |
|---|---|---|
| **Scope** | everything under current dir | just the named file |
| **Precision** | broad — stages all changes | surgical — exactly what you pick |
| **Risk** | high — can stage secrets/junk | low — explicit choice |
| **Untracked files** | stages new files too | only if you name them |
| **Best for** | all changes belong together | separating mixed work into commits |

sections.title: Staging Tools at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|git add .|~Stage everything|all modified + new|fast but risky|review with status first
emerald|git add file|~Stage one file|surgical control|focused commits|name exactly what you want
amber|git add -p|~Stage hunks|chunk by chunk|split debug from real code|interactive patch mode
violet|git add -u|~Modified + deleted only|skips new untracked|update tracked files|won't add new files

sections.title: Risky: git add . without looking
sections.content:
```bash
# Reflexive 'add everything' with no review
git add .
git commit -m "work"
# Oops: this just staged & committed application-local.properties
# with the production DB password, plus the whole target/ folder
```

sections.title: Deliberate: review, then stage what belongs together
sections.content:
```bash
git status                       # see what's changed first
git add src/main/java/com/example/service/OrderService.java
git commit -m "feat: add order cancellation"

# Separate, unrelated bug fix -> its own commit
git add src/main/java/com/example/repo/CustomerRepository.java
git commit -m "fix: case-insensitive customer lookup"

# Mixed changes in ONE file? stage only the right hunks
git add -p OrderService.java
```
*Focused commits make history reviewable and easy to revert — and keep secrets out.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **`git add .` without `git status`**: easy way to commit secrets or build output — always review first.
- **Adding before `.gitignore` exists**: stages `target/`, `.idea/`, etc.; set up `.gitignore` on day one.
- **Never using `git add -p`**: staging whole files even when only half belongs in the commit makes history tangled.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`git add`** stages changes into the index for the next commit.
- **`git add .`** = everything under the current dir (new files too); **`git add filename`** = just that file.
- **`git add -p`** stages individual hunks — split unrelated changes.
- **`git add -u`** stages modified/deleted tracked files, not new ones.
- **Always `git status` first** to avoid staging secrets or junk.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The git add command moves changes from your working directory into the staging area, which is like a preparation zone for your next commit. The key difference is scope. Git add with a dot stages everything in your current directory and all subdirectories — every modified file and every new file. It's fast, but it's risky because you can stage things you didn't mean to. Git add with a filename stages only that one file, giving you precise control. In a real project, say I'm on a feature branch and I've edited OrderService to add a method, but I also fixed an unrelated bug in CustomerRepository. Those solve different problems, so I don't want them in the same commit. I'd run git add OrderService dot java, commit the feature, then git add CustomerRepository dot java and commit the fix separately. That keeps history clean. One thing freshers miss is git add dash p, patch mode, which shows you each changed chunk and lets you stage it or skip it — really handy when you've got debug print statements mixed in with real code. The mistake I see all the time is people typing git add dot without running git status first, and they end up committing their properties file with the production database password in it. So my habit is always git status before git add.

questions.question: What information does 'git status' show?
questions.title: Understanding git status
questions.direct_answer: **`git status`** reports the current state of your repo: **staged** changes ready for the next commit, **unstaged** changes (tracked files you've modified but not added), and **untracked** files (new files Git doesn't know about yet). It also shows your branch and whether you're ahead/behind the remote. **`git status -s`** gives a compact two-letter format.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate has the habit of checking repo state before staging/committing/switching and understands the three file categories
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Committing without checking status and shipping debug code, half-finished work, or unintended files
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention git status -s for compact output and the meaning of a clean working tree before switching branches or pulling

sections.title: Your Repository's Dashboard
sections.content:
**`git status`** is your situational-awareness tool — like a car dashboard you check before driving. It sorts your files into three buckets: **staged** changes (ready for the next commit), **unstaged** changes (tracked files you've modified but not added), and **untracked** files (brand-new files Git isn't tracking yet).

It also prints your current branch and whether it's ahead or behind the remote. Pros run it constantly — before staging, before committing, after pulling, before switching branches — because it tells you both what's about to be committed and what you still need to decide. A **clean working tree** means there's nothing to commit, so it's safe to switch branches or pull.

sections.title: The Three File States
sections.content:
emerald|Staged|~Ready to commit|already git added|goes in next commit|shown in green
amber|Unstaged|~Modified, tracked|edited but not added|needs git add|shown in red
blue|Untracked|~Brand new|Git doesn't know it|needs git add to track|shown in red
violet|Clean tree|~Nothing to commit|all changes committed|safe to switch/pull|'working tree clean'

sections.title: Reading git status (full and short)
sections.content:
```bash
git status
# On branch feature/order-processing
# Your branch is up to date with 'origin/feature/order-processing'.
#
# Changes to be committed:        <- STAGED (green)
#   modified:   OrderService.java
#
# Changes not staged for commit:  <- UNSTAGED (red)
#   modified:   application.properties
#
# Untracked files:                <- UNTRACKED (red)
#   PaymentProcessor.java

# Compact two-letter format
git status -s
# M  OrderService.java        (left col = staged)
#  M application.properties   (right col = unstaged)
# ?? PaymentProcessor.java    (untracked)
```

sections.title: Trap: committing blind without checking status
sections.content:
```bash
# No status check -> no idea what's actually staged
git add .
git commit -m "done"
# Shipped a leftover debug line and a half-edited config file
# git log now has a commit you'll have to clean up later
```

sections.title: Habit: status before staging and committing
sections.content:
```bash
git status            # what changed, and in which bucket?
git diff              # review the actual unstaged edits
git add OrderService.java
git status            # confirm ONLY what you intend is staged
git commit -m "feat: add order cancellation"
```
*Running status before and after staging is the cheapest insurance against a messy commit.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Skipping status before commit**: easiest way to commit debug prints or commented-out code.
- **Ignoring untracked files**: they're often new source files you forgot to add — or files that need a `.gitignore` entry.
- **Not knowing the colors/columns**: green/left = staged, red/right = unstaged; confusing them means committing the wrong thing.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Three buckets** — staged, unstaged, untracked.
- **Staged (green)** goes in the next commit; **unstaged/untracked (red)** doesn't.
- **`git status -s`** is a compact two-letter view (M, A, D, ??).
- **Clean working tree** = safe to switch branches or pull.
- **Run it constantly** — before staging, committing, pulling, switching.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Git status shows the current state of your working directory and staging area. It sorts your files into three groups: staged changes, in green, that are ready for your next commit; unstaged changes, in red, that you've modified but haven't added yet; and untracked files, also in red, that are brand new and Git doesn't know about. In a typical workflow, say I'm building a feature and I've edited OrderService and created a new PaymentProcessor class. Running git status shows OrderService as modified but not staged, and PaymentProcessor as untracked. That tells me I need to decide what to stage. After I run git add on OrderService and check status again, now it shows up in green under changes to be committed, while PaymentProcessor is still untracked because I haven't added it. When status says working tree clean, that means everything's committed and it's safe to switch branches or pull. The mistake freshers make is not running status before committing — you might have left a debug print statement in or modified a config file with test credentials, and status catches that before it goes into history. I run it almost reflexively, before and after staging. There's also git status dash s for a short format that just shows letter codes like M for modified, which is faster to scan when you've got a lot of files.

questions.question: What makes a good Git commit message, and what are conventional commit conventions?
questions.title: Good Git Commit Messages
questions.direct_answer: A good commit message is concise, written in the **imperative mood** ("Add validation", not "Added"), and explains *what* and ideally *why*. **Conventional Commits** add a structured prefix — `type(scope): description` with types like `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `refactor` — so tools can auto-generate changelogs and pick the next version (`feat`→minor, `fix`→patch, breaking→major). Follow the **50/72 rule** for subject and body width.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate treats commit messages as documentation for teammates and tools, not a formality
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Vague messages ('fix', 'wip', 'changes') and past tense ('Added'), which are useless for git log/git blame later
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the 50/72 rule and that conventional commits power semantic-release for automated changelogs and version bumps

sections.title: A Commit Message Is Documentation, Not a Formality
sections.content:
A **commit message** is permanent documentation of why a change was made. Treat your history like a medical record: when a bug hits production, you'll use **`git log`** and **`git blame`** to trace it to a commit, and the message must tell you what that change intended.

Write the subject in **imperative mood** — "Add user authentication", not "Added" — because Git itself does ("Merge branch", "Revert commit"). **Conventional Commits** add machine-readable prefixes (`feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, `refactor:`). That structure powers automation: tools scan the history, group commits into a changelog, and bump the version automatically (a `feat` → minor, a `fix` → patch).

sections.title: Anatomy of a Conventional Commit
sections.content:
blue|Type|~The category|feat, fix, docs|refactor, test, chore|drives the version bump
emerald|Scope|~The component|in parentheses|(auth), (orders)|optional but helpful
amber|Subject|~Imperative, <=50|'add', not 'added'|lowercase, no period|what the commit does
violet|Body & footer|~The why|wrap at ~72|explains reasoning|BREAKING CHANGE / issue refs

sections.title: Step 1 — Pick the Type and Scope
sections.content:
Choose the prefix that matches the change; add a scope in parentheses to name the affected component (`auth`, `orders`, `payment`).

| Type | Use it for | SemVer effect |
|---|---|---|
| `feat` | new user-facing capability | minor |
| `fix` | corrected behavior / bug | patch |
| `refactor` | restructure, no behavior change | none |
| `docs` | docs/README/JavaDoc only | none |
| `test` | adding/updating tests | none |
| `chore` | deps, build, CI | none |
| `feat!` / `BREAKING CHANGE` | incompatible change | major |

sections.title: Step 2 — Write the Message (50/72 rule)
sections.content:
```bash
# Subject: imperative, lowercase, <=50 chars, no trailing period
git commit -m "feat(orders): add order cancellation endpoint"
git commit -m "fix(auth): prevent duplicate user registration"
git commit -m "docs(readme): add Docker setup instructions"

# Body explains WHY (wrap at ~72 chars); footer references issues
git commit -m "fix(payment): handle timeout in Stripe API calls" \
           -m "Stripe occasionally took >5s and the call failed silently." \
           -m "Added a timeout plus retry with backoff. Resolves #234."

# Breaking change -> major bump
git commit -m "feat(api)!: require POST for order status updates" \
           -m "BREAKING CHANGE: GET is no longer accepted; clients must use POST."
```

sections.title: Useless messages you'll regret in six months
sections.content:
```bash
git commit -m "fixed stuff"
git commit -m "wip"
git commit -m "changes"
git commit -m "Added login feature"   # past tense, no type
# git log is now noise; git blame tells you nothing about intent
```

sections.title: Clear, conventional, searchable messages
sections.content:
```bash
git commit -m "fix(auth): prevent SQL injection in login query"
git commit -m "feat(orders): add order cancellation endpoint"
git commit -m "refactor(repo): extract query logic into specifications"
# git log --grep '^feat' lists every feature; changelog generates itself
```
*Specific, imperative, prefixed messages make history a tool, not a wall of text.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Vague messages**: "fixed bug" says nothing — which bug? Be specific.
- **Past tense**: write "Add"/"Fix", not "Added"/"Fixed" — complete the sentence "This commit will…".
- **WIP commits**: use `git stash` for temporary saves instead of `wip`/`asdf` messages.
- **No 'why' for tricky changes**: the diff shows *what*; add a body for the *why*.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Imperative mood** — "Add feature", matching Git's own style.
- **`type(scope): description`** — `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `refactor`, `test`, `chore`.
- **`feat`→minor, `fix`→patch, breaking→major** under semantic versioning.
- **50/72 rule** — subject ≤50 chars, body wrapped at ~72.
- **Conventional commits enable automation** — changelogs and version bumps.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A good commit message explains what the commit does, clearly and specifically. You write it in the imperative mood, like a command — Add feature, not Added feature — because that matches how Git itself writes things like Merge branch. Conventional commits take this further by adding a structured prefix. You start with a type: feat for a new feature, fix for a bug fix, docs for documentation, refactor for code changes that don't change behavior. Then optionally a scope in parentheses naming the component. So a real message looks like feat, orders, colon, add order cancellation endpoint, or fix, auth, colon, prevent SQL injection in login query. The structure isn't just for humans — tools can scan the history, count how many feat and fix commits there are, and automatically generate a changelog and pick the next version number. A feat bumps the minor version, a fix bumps the patch, and a breaking change, flagged with an exclamation mark or a BREAKING CHANGE line, bumps the major. For complex changes you add a body paragraph explaining why, since the diff already shows what. The biggest mistake freshers make is vague messages like fixed stuff or wip, which are useless when you're hunting a bug six months later with git log. Be specific. The other is past tense — Git's convention is imperative. And there's the fifty seventy-two rule: keep the subject under fifty characters and wrap the body around seventy-two for readability in the terminal.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'git diff' and 'git diff --staged'?
questions.title: git diff vs git diff --staged
questions.direct_answer: **`git diff`** shows **unstaged** changes — your working directory compared to the staging area (what you'd still need to `git add`). **`git diff --staged`** (alias `--cached`) shows **staged** changes — the staging area compared to your last commit (what's actually going into the next commit). **`git diff HEAD`** shows both combined versus the last commit.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the three-tree model well enough to know which diff shows which layer, and reviews before committing
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Running git diff after git add, seeing nothing, and being confused — staged changes need --staged
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention git diff HEAD for the full picture and that --cached is an older alias for --staged

sections.title: Two Diffs for Two Checkpoints
sections.content:
**`git diff`** shows line-by-line changes, but *which* changes depends on the flag. Plain **`git diff`** compares your **working directory** to the **staging area**, so it shows **unstaged** edits — "what have I changed since I last staged?" **`git diff --staged`** (also **`--cached`**) compares the **staging area** to your **last commit**, showing **staged** changes — "what will actually go into my next commit?"

Think of it as a two-checkpoint review: `git diff` is checkpoint one (working vs staged), `git diff --staged` is checkpoint two (staged vs committed). This split exists because Git's three-tree model lets you stage some changes while still editing others. Pros review both before committing.

sections.title: git diff vs git diff --staged
sections.content:
| Aspect | `git diff` | `git diff --staged` |
|---|---|---|
| **Compares** | working dir vs staging area | staging area vs last commit |
| **Shows** | changes NOT yet staged | changes already staged |
| **Run it** | before `git add` | after `git add`, before commit |
| **Empty when** | nothing unstaged left | nothing staged |
| **Purpose** | preview what you'll stage | review what you'll commit |

sections.title: Diff Variants in the Three-Tree Model
sections.content:
blue|git diff|~Working vs staged|unstaged edits|run before git add|preview what to stage
emerald|git diff --staged|~Staged vs commit|what's about to commit|run before git commit|aka --cached
amber|git diff HEAD|~All vs last commit|staged + unstaged|full session picture|total progress
violet|git diff --stat|~Summary only|files + line counts|no full hunks|quick scan

sections.title: The confusing moment: diff shows nothing after add
sections.content:
```bash
git add .
git diff           # prints NOTHING
# Fresher: 'where did my changes go?!'
# Reason: plain git diff only shows UNSTAGED changes,
# and you just staged everything.
```

sections.title: The right tool: review staged, then commit
sections.content:
```bash
git diff               # review unstaged edits first
git add -p OrderService.java   # stage only the right hunks
git diff               # now shows only what's STILL unstaged
git diff --staged      # shows exactly what's going into the commit
git diff HEAD          # everything vs last commit (full picture)
git commit -m "feat: add order cancellation"
```
*Review `--staged` right before committing to catch anything you didn't mean to include.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **`git diff` after `git add`**: shows nothing because everything is staged — use `--staged`.
- **Committing without reviewing**: skipping `git diff --staged` lets debug code and stray edits slip into history.
- **Skimming large diffs**: rushing past hundreds of lines hides accidental deletions or leftover debug code.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`git diff`** = unstaged (working vs staging); run before `git add`.
- **`git diff --staged`/`--cached`** = staged (staging vs last commit); run before commit.
- **`git diff HEAD`** = all changes vs last commit.
- **`git diff --stat`** = file/line summary for a quick scan.
- **Two-checkpoint review** catches mistakes before they enter history.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Git diff shows line-by-line changes, but what it shows depends on the flag. Plain git diff compares your working directory — the actual files on disk — to the staging area, so it shows changes you've made but haven't staged yet. That's your first review point, before you run git add. Git diff with dash dash staged compares the staging area to your last commit, so it shows what's already staged and will go into your next commit. That's your second review point, after staging but before committing. Here's the workflow: say I edit OrderService, adding a new method and changing an existing one. I run git diff and see both. I stage only the new method with git add dash p. Now git diff shows just the existing-method change, because that's still unstaged, while git diff dash dash staged shows the new method I staged. That separation lets me build focused commits even from mixed changes. The mistake freshers make is running git diff right after git add dot and getting confused that nothing appears — that's because everything's been staged, so there are no unstaged changes left, and you need the dash dash staged flag. There's also git diff HEAD, which shows everything, staged and unstaged together, compared to your last commit, for the full picture. And dash dash cached is just an older name for dash dash staged.

followup_questions: What does git diff HEAD show that the other two don't?
Why does git diff show nothing right after git add?

questions.question: What does 'git commit --amend' do, and when should you use it?
questions.title: Amending the Last Commit with git commit --amend
questions.direct_answer: **`git commit --amend`** replaces your most recent commit — to fix its message or add forgotten staged files — by creating a **brand-new commit object with a different SHA**. Because the SHA changes, only amend commits that **haven't been pushed** to a shared branch; amending pushed history forces a `--force` push and breaks teammates who already pulled it.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands amend rewrites history (new SHA) and knows the golden rule against rewriting shared history
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Amending an already-pushed commit, then force-pushing and giving teammates divergent history
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that --amend creates a new SHA so Git sees a different commit, and use --no-edit when only adding files

sections.title: Amend Replaces the Last Commit, It Doesn't Edit It
sections.content:
**`git commit --amend`** tells Git to replace your most recent commit entirely rather than add a new one. It takes whatever is currently **staged**, combines it with the previous commit's changes, and creates a **new commit object with a different SHA**. The old commit drops off your branch (it lingers in Git's object database for a while).

It's perfect for fixing a typo in the message or adding a file you forgot to stage. The catch freshers miss: because the SHA changes, Git treats the amended commit as a **completely different commit**. If teammates already pulled the original, their history now diverges from yours — which is why the **golden rule** is: never amend commits already pushed to a shared branch like `main` or `develop`.

sections.title: When Amend Is Safe
sections.content:
emerald|Safe|~Local only|commit not pushed|fix message or add files|new SHA is fine
rose|Dangerous|~Already pushed|on a shared branch|needs --force to push|breaks teammates
amber|How it works|~Replace, not edit|new commit object|different SHA|old commit drops off
blue|Handy flags|~Common uses|--no-edit keeps message|stage files first|then --amend

sections.title: Amending in Practice
sections.content:
```bash
# Committed with a typo and forgot a file
git add UserService.java
git commit -m "Add user validaton logic"   # typo!

# Stage the forgotten file, then amend
git add UserValidator.java
git commit --amend -m "Add user validation logic"
# -> ONE commit now contains both files, with the fixed message

# Only fixing the message (no new files):
git commit --amend -m "Better commit message"

# Adding files but keeping the existing message:
git add ForgottenFile.java
git commit --amend --no-edit
```

sections.title: Wrong: amend a commit that's already pushed
sections.content:
```bash
git push origin feature-auth      # commit is now shared
git commit --amend -m "better msg" # new SHA, diverges from remote
git push origin feature-auth
# ! [rejected] non-fast-forward
git push --force origin feature-auth
# Teammates who pulled the old commit now have broken, divergent history
```

sections.title: Right: amend only local commits, else make a new one
sections.content:
```bash
# Confirm the commit isn't on the remote yet
git log origin/feature-auth..HEAD   # if it lists your commit, it's local

# Local -> safe to amend
git commit --amend --no-edit

# Already pushed -> DON'T amend; add a normal follow-up commit
git commit -m "fix: correct validation logic"
git push origin feature-auth
```
*If it's shared, a new commit is cleaner and never rewrites anyone else's history.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Amending after pushing**: leads to a rejected push, then a risky `--force` that breaks teammates.
- **Forgetting to stage first**: `--amend` only uses what's staged, so unstaged files won't be included.
- **Amending repeatedly**: chaining many amends on one commit is messy — prefer separate commits or an interactive rebase later.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Amend replaces the last commit** with a new object and a new SHA.
- **Use it** to fix the message or add forgotten staged files.
- **Golden rule** — never amend commits already pushed to a shared branch.
- **`--no-edit`** keeps the existing message when only adding files.
- **If it's pushed, make a new commit** instead of force-pushing.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Git commit amend lets you modify the very last commit you made. It's useful in two main situations: fixing a typo in your commit message, or adding files you forgot to stage before you committed. The important thing to understand is that amend doesn't actually edit the existing commit. Instead, it creates a brand-new commit with a different SHA hash that replaces the old one, and the old commit drops off your branch. For example, if I committed with a typo in the message, I can run git commit amend with a corrected message and Git replaces that commit. Or if I forgot to include a validator class, I stage it with git add and run git commit amend, optionally with no-edit to keep the same message, and now both files are in one clean commit. The critical part is when you should use it. Only amend commits that haven't been pushed to a shared branch yet. The reason is that amending changes the commit's SHA, so Git sees it as a completely different commit. If your teammates already pulled the original, their history diverges from yours, and when you push the amended version Git rejects it unless you force-push, which overwrites the remote and breaks everyone who had the old commit. That's the golden rule — don't rewrite shared history. So if the commit is already pushed, I just make a new follow-up commit instead. It's cleaner and it doesn't disrupt the team.
